en: Preface to the Direct Explanation of the Verses on the Contemplation of Conditions Aroused by Mindfulness of the Buddha:
This single gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha is the grand mainstay of the net of all Buddhas' teachings and the essential entrance to the Pure Land.
Originally proclaimed at Vulture Peak, the transmission of its lineage reached China beginning with Mount Lu during the Jin dynasty.

Upon reaching the Sui period, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi emerged and propagated the single method of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*). Thereupon, the great framework was raised aloft and the net of the teachings was spread wide.
My Buddha’s broad and long tongue-mark then completely covered the land of Zhendan (China).
During the Sui dynasty, there was Zhi-er, the first patriarch of Tiantai, who composed the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*) pointing the way back to the Pure Land.

Having achieved the three stages of non-retrogression in the supramundane realm, he relied upon this essential merit in a place where the karmic conditions of sentient beings in the Dharma-ending age were easily met.
In each of his treatises on the Buddha-remembrance (*nien-fo*), he decisively shattered the multitude of doubts and elucidated the profound mysteries;
he was truly a master craftsman who presided over the great tradition of the Pure Land. I reflect that the practice of Buddhism is more difficult than that of Confucianism;

to revitalize the collapsing standards of this degenerate age and to succeed to the Dharma-lineage of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa—this great matter (*mahā-kārya*) certainly cannot be undertaken by anyone other than a sage. First...
The Venerable Xian considers that the First Patriarch of Tiantai was indeed the reincarnation of Śākyamuni;

this is truly worthy of belief. Subsequently, there were those who arose to continue the Tiantai tradition: for instance, Feixi of the Tang dynasty composed the *Bao Wang Lun* (Treasure King Treatise);

Youtan of the Song dynasty composed the *Bao Jian* (Jade Mirror); and Tianru of the Yuan dynasty composed the *Hui Wu Wen* (Questions and Answers). Furthermore, there are others such as Zongjing and Gong.
According to what can be discussed, the lineage holders throughout the successive dynasties have produced a vast wealth of writings, which I find difficult to recount in full.

However, upon reaching the Ming dynasty, the Great Master Ouyi emerged from Lingfeng and compiled the work *Ten Essentials of Pure Land* (*Jingtu shiyao*), which may truly be called a successor to this tradition.

Tiantai synthesized these teachings into their great consummation. Yet, in remote villages and narrow alleys, the elderly, children, and women know only to practice the eight-line verse of contemplation;
they have not been able to master the entirety of the great treatises—this is truly lamentable.

There are even those who, fearing the underworld for lack of funds, take the single phrase "Namo Amitābha" as currency to pay their debts. Alas! This is like using a bright pearl to buy a mere pellet.

O Sparrow-Ear, you do not know that the single gate of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) is the wisdom-sword that cuts across birth and death, and the swift sail that directly exits the dark realm of the underworld.
To become a Buddha and deliver sentient beings depends upon this one thought; to be born in the lotus and escape the kalpa depends upon this one thought.
Are you willing to take this thought as currency? Indeed, thoughts have no magnitude; one must simply realize their perfect nature. As the *Contemplation Sūtra* says: "All..."
The Buddha, the Tathāgata, is the body of the Dharma-realm; he enters into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings. Therefore, know that the Buddha’s face is turned toward all sentient beings.
To recite even a single phrase of the Buddha's name can destroy the karmic obstructions of all sentient beings, who are one's adversaries.
To recite a single phrase of the Buddha’s name can shake the wisdom-reeds of all sentient beings.
When karmic obstructions are destroyed, the land does not wait to be purified before it becomes pure; thus, there is birth in the Pure Land.

When the sprouts of wisdom are shaken, the flowers do not wait to bloom before they blossom; thus, one is supported by the body of a lotus flower. Since the world is vast and boundless, this single thought-moment—
The power of this [recitation] is likewise boundless. As sentient beings emerge from the cycle of existence without end, so too the power of this single thought-moment is inexhaustible.
One should know that by being able to hold the Buddha’s name, even reciting it but once, the seed of Bodhi is planted forever for long kalpas.
Its towering merit is equal in measure to the Dharma-realm. Thus, by offering a single stick of incense or a single flower before the Buddha, one is immediately able to...
Universally making offerings to all sentient beings, one enables them to be permeated by this floral fragrance, so that they may equally obtain the provisions for attaining Buddhahood in the future.
Seeking the real through the illusory—wherein nothing illusory is not true—is the perfect understanding; only through mindfulness of the Buddha can one truly gain power.
Alas! The merit of this single Dharma-gate is truly difficult to conceive.

Herein, I borrow eight lines from the *Guanjing* (Contemplation Sutra) to guide those who follow their respective practices, desiring that they all together transcend to the Pure Land and come to believe in the existence of the single gate of Buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*).
I pray that those with aspirations for this path will read this compilation and further study the *Ten Essentials of Lingfeng*.
Thus, the path to the Pure Land can be directly realized through self-awakening in this very moment.
Recorded respectfully by the junior scholar Zhang Yuan of Shannan during the first month of summer in the Jiashu year of the Tongzhi era.
*Direct Explanation of the Verses on the Contemplation of Amitābha: The Origins of the Practice of Nianfo*.
Compiled by Zhang Yuanqian Shishi of Southern Shan;
edited by Zhang Mengxian Luyou Shishi;
and compiled by Lou Renshen Jingshan Shishi of Western Shan.
Edited by Zhao Hongwen and Xu Zhai Shi Na;
with Jie Su and Lianfang.
Amitābha Buddha’s body is golden in color.

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Buddha" means awakening (*buddha*). He awakens to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and furthermore, he is able to awaken sentient beings, just as one awakens from sleep or a dream;

therefore, he is named Buddha. Moreover, possessing both all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), he has emerged from the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Having awakened to the nature and characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmas*), he is able to awaken himself and also awaken others.
All sentient beings awaken like those emerging from sleep or like lotus flowers blooming; therefore, they are called Buddhas. Furthermore, awakening has three meanings:
self-awakening, awakening others, and the fulfillment of awakening.

(Commentary: There are three kinds of wisdom. Because self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of awakening share the same meaning, all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) is perfected in the realm of the Arhat; the wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākārajñā*) is perfected in the realm of the Bodhisattva; and when the wisdom of all aspects is fully perfected, the Dharma-body fills the Dharma-realm, which is the realm of the Buddha.

Furthermore, upon entering the realm of the Arhat, the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are eliminated and all-encompassing wisdom is perfected, yet a single residue of ignorance remains, lingering as a form of knowing.

Upon entering the realm of the Bodhisattva, the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are eliminated and the wisdom of the paths and their fruits (*mārgajñatā*) is perfected. Since this wisdom flows from the various paths, ignorance has already been shattered and the cognitive obstructions no longer remain; however, though they are broken, they are not yet entirely exhausted. If one enters the realm of the Buddha, they are shattered completely.)

Clarity and quiescent wisdom shine forth together; this is called the perfection of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) and knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñā*). Furthermore, afflictions are the internal obstruction of ignorance, while ignorance is the external obstruction of afflictions. Arhats have not yet fully perfected the seeds of the Path.

However, because they have only transcended internal obstacles but not yet transcended external obstacles, they remain within the realm of sentient beings' afflictions; fearing that they might again become deluded and attached, they dare not re-enter once they have emerged. They are only able to awaken themselves, but are not yet able to awaken other sentient beings.

The Bodhisattva has already perfected the seeds of the Way (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). By means of various causes and conditions that assist the Way, they can counteract the delusions and attachments of ignorance; thus, they are able to enter universally into the dust and toil of the world without them again becoming obstacles. Being able to awaken themselves, they are also able to awaken others. The Buddha possesses the perfect understanding of both self and others, having realized ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*).

In this state, all delusions are entirely wisdom, and all obstacles are entirely virtue. This is what constitutes the fulfillment of awakening. Regarding the three types of wisdom mentioned above, they are respectively assigned to three types of persons. To make it easy for people to understand, I have distinguished them according to the gradual sequence of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*).

If one were to rely on the Sudden Teaching (*tathāgata-śāsana*), one attains Buddhahood through mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) without passing through gradual stages. Why is this? Because mindfulness of the Buddha is the direct seed of the Buddha. It is simply a matter of opening and developing samādhi; as soon as one is mindful, [one realizes it].
He enters the Buddha-wisdom and transcends the various stages of the Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (i.e., his position within the ten stages is that of the first stage).
*Amitābha* is translated and explained as "Immeasurable," which is the Buddha of Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*) mentioned in the *Contemplation Sūtra*.

Regarding the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas—their wisdom, merit, compassion, transformative guidance, supernormal powers, skillful means, and their Dharma bodies—all these are indeed said to be immeasurable;
however, as for the length of their lifespans, each follows its own original vow.
Amitābha dwells in the world with profound vows, and his lifespan is likewise called immeasurable; therefore, he is named Amitābha.

Alas! Since Amitābha dwells in the world, Śākyamuni may enter parinirvāṇa. Those who practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name should cultivate the visualization of him as a substitute for their own Teacher. (100)
The body is golden in color. There are three meanings to the "body," namely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Regarding the aspect of the Dharma-body alone, it is the fundamental principle through which all Buddhas bestow their teachings. If those who practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) understand this meaning, their faculties will naturally benefit themselves;
their birth and future realms in a future life will differ from those of the middle and lower capacities. This is a vital point.
This must not be overlooked; I shall describe it point by point. As for the *dharmakāya*: it is the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* and the Great *Nirvāṇa*.
When the mind of arising and ceasing is extinguished, the mind of *tathatā* manifests, and this is termed the *dharmakāya*.
This body has no land from which it comes and no land to which it goes. It is the body of the fundamental *dharmadhātu*, pervading all things. Why is this? Because the substance of the mind...

It is fundamentally quiescent; therefore, it is called *tathatā*. Grasping is also one's own mind, and relinquishing is also one's own mind. There is another verse that says: "The mind takes only its own mind as an object;
thus the mind itself becomes non-characteristic (*animitta*). From this non-characteristic, things arise in turn, and thus the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*) comes into being."
The entire world is an illusory phenomenon; it is all created by one’s own mind. Apart from the mind, the mind itself is empty. Upon whom can these illusory phenomena depend?
Fundamentally, there is no mark of a sentient being; how then could any phenomena arise? Since phenomena themselves do not arise, upon what conditions could the world be produced?
This is the wondrous True Suchness, the single path to the gate of Nirvana. Nirvana is fundamentally like this; this is precisely—
The Tathāgatagarbha: all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions equally transcend through this and equally realize the ultimate.
One should know that this wondrous True Suchness (Tathatā) is the fundamental wisdom that is omnipresent and omnipotent, the Dharma-body of equality of all Tathāgatas.
For those who practice Buddha-remembrance, if they penetrate this meaning, then in a single thought-moment being with the Buddha is itself the accomplishment of a single thought-moment of Buddhahood.

Wisdom: when every thought-moment dwells upon the Buddha, one immediately achieves moment-to-moment wisdom (*kṣaṇa-kṣaṇa-jñāna*). When mindfulness reaches the point where there is nothing to be mindful of, mindfulness enters into non-mindfulness (*amanasikāra*).

Suddenly, through this mindfulness, one arrives at the liberation of the emptiness of the mind; all phenomena are simultaneously stilled. At that very moment, one glimpses Amitābha appearing before one.
Therefore, know that he is none other than the Amitābha of one’s own original nature. Since he is born from the Pure Land, know that he is indeed *cittamātra* (mind-only).
The mind is the pure land. One awakens to the error of discriminating between self and other, and attains the wondrous principle that all response and resonance is but the mind itself.
However, this is merely cultivation on the stage of ordinary beings; a single thought-moment is extremely subtle.
If one does not rely upon the Buddhas of the fruition stage to fix their mindfulness, can the power of this single thought truly break through the heavy obstacles of ignorance? Can it truly...
Can one sever and transcend the afflictions accumulated over kalpas?

Once one has attained the wondrous limit of True Suchness (tathatā) and fixes the mind upon a single Buddha, then that Buddha-mind at the stage of fruition is not necessarily another’s mind, and the mind of mindfulness at the causal stage is not necessarily one’s own mind;
in sum, it is the perfection of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Furthermore, according to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Śākyamuni...

When one attains perfect enlightenment, within that very body one universally perceives all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment, and even universally perceives all sentient beings entering nirvana—all are universally perceived within this single body.
This is the meaning of the dharmatā pervading the entire body; it serves as proof of the omnipresence of the Dharmakāya. As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha-body fills..."

The Dharma-realm universally manifests before all sentient beings; responding to conditions and meeting with those who seek it, there is nowhere it does not reach, yet it eternally abides upon this very seat of Bodhi.
To know that the Dharma-body of Śākyamuni is thus is to know the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas, and it is also to know the Dharma-body of Amitābha.
As the Sūtra says: "All Tathāgatas are of one and the same [Dharma-body]."
The Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is one mind and one wisdom; its powers and fearlessnesses are likewise so. The above all refer to the Dharma-body.
Generally, the Dharma-body has three meanings: first, the meaning of equality and non-discrimination; second, the meaning of a quiescent essence that is omnipresent;
third, the meaning of the nature of true thusness (tathatā), which is immovable and indestructible, yet capable of functioning in accordance with conditions. Therefore, this Dharma-body—
Expanded, its origin is the Dharma-realm; contracted, it is simply Mind-only.

Because the mind of the Dharma-realm possesses the body of the Dharma-realm, it immediately constructs the inconceivable conditions of the Dharma-realm. Thus, once the conditions of the Dharma-realm manifest, the body of the Dharma-realm is revealed.
Whether as possessing or as constructing, both are beyond thought. That which is inconceivable is precisely this:
"Mind-only" is the gate of contemplation for the wise. One knows that my single mind possesses the power to create the entire Dharma-realm; both this creation and this possession are mind-only.
Fundamentally inconceivable, because it is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way, one establishes the three inconceivable contemplations.
Only then is this the true path for manifesting the Dharma-realm and reaching the wondrous intent of Mind-only. Now, as for those three contemplations:
This is precisely the perfect contemplation (*parivarta*). Why is it called "inconceivable" (*acintya*)? It is not that it is inherently inconceivable;
rather, it is simply that it cannot be conceived. This is because the true mind of quiescent extinction (*śānta-tathatā-citta*) cannot be entered through conceptual thought.

Within this inconceivability lies the very path for the arising of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). Now, this gate of inconceivable mindfulness and that gate of contemplation are— [no difference].
The two are not distinct. One must necessarily attain the inconceivable; then, although the Dharma-body of Amitābha does not manifest, it manifests.
My mind of mindfulness of the Buddha is revealed through primordial wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). This is called truly mindful of the Dharma-body Buddha.

This single Dharma-body is realized to its ultimate extent only by Buddhas and Buddhas. As for the Reward-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), it is that which is retributed through the adornment of meritorious virtues.
Body. This body originally arises from the power of vows to gather in sentient beings;

thus, it manifests as the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) of adorned merit, and is also the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) of a Bodhisattva. As it is said: "The eyes are as broad as the four great oceans;
the ūrṇā-hair is as broad as five Mount Sumerus. Within a single body, there are eighty-four thousand rays of light each."

When the marks and signs are clarified, the dimensions of the body likewise become boundless; only great Bodhisattvas are able to perceive this, which is what is called the *sambhogakāya* (Body of Exalted Attributes).
As for the *nirmāṇakāya* (Response Body), it refers to the bodies manifested through transformation throughout all worlds.
Sometimes he manifests a body sixteen feet tall; sometimes he manifests a body eight feet tall. His body responds solely according to the size of sentient beings' own bodies.
His body is endowed with the thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary signs, and a halo surrounds his neck.
Furthermore, the extent of the light surrounding his body varies in its manifestation;
however, the single mark manifested by the *uṣṇīṣa* on his crown is further designated as the "Unseen Crown. Even great Bodhisattvas can never perceive its limits.
Is it not therefore that the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are also seen as being boundless? This body [attains] the four fruits.
The disciples and those sentient beings with whom there is a karmic affinity from former lives are all able to see it; this is what is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-transformation body).
The body indicated by this phrase here is the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) adorned with merits.
As for its golden color, it is an indestructible color.
The marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and their radiant light are peerless.
The *Amitābha-dhyāna-sūtra* states that the Buddha’s recompense body (*vipākakāya*) possesses eighty-four thousand marks.
Within each mark, there are eighty-four thousand secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*). Within each secondary sign, there are further eighty-four thousand rays of light.
Each and every ray of light shines universally upon sentient beings in the ten directions who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, gathering them in and never abandoning them.
Even the transformation Buddhas manifested within these lights cannot be fully described.

What the sages of old said—that if a person practices mindfulness of the Buddha, a transformation Tathāgata will dwell upon their crown—is indeed true; through his great vow of compassion, such wondrous efficacy has been accomplished.

The power of his virtue is as lofty and majestic as this; this constitutes the "Distinguished Excellence" (zunte). "Lun" means category; it signifies that there is no longer any category or equal to him.
These three characters form a single unit, penetrating the joints between the upper and lower [sections]. Such are the Buddha’s radiant light and marks of excellence.

Regarding the statement that each is divided into eighty-four thousand: this is because sentient beings possess eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) and their bodies have eighty-four thousand pores;
therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, they likewise each come to possess eighty-four thousand marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of radiance.
Furthermore, according to the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the halo of that Buddha is as vast as ten billion [worlds].
Within the circular halo, there are transformed Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and even countless transformed Bodhisattvas.
How can the circular halo be so vast? One should know that this great circular halo is the collective radiance of the Sambhogakāya Buddha.
As for the eighty-four thousand rays of light manifested within each of these marks and signs, they are...
This reveals the distinct radiances of the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. Whether collectively or individually, each possesses the secret and wondrous gateways through which transformation Buddhas manifest.
How could such an ocean of the nature of merit and virtue, thus adorned, ever be contained within the scope of thought?
The white curl of hair (ūrṇā-kośa) winds like five Mount Sumerus.
"Mount Sumeru" is the name of a mountain located in the midst of the four great continents.

It rises from the great ocean, piercing through the sun and moon, and towers three hundred and thirty-six thousand *li* high; its circumference is likewise the same. Furthermore, as for the mountain...
The middle sections of its four sides are all the palaces of the celestial kings. Each of the Four Great Heavenly Kings occupies one side and presides over one continent;
thus, these four continents are divided into the four quarters of the world. This division occurs because of the height and breadth of this mountain.
Now, the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows of the Sambhogakāya Buddha curls to the right, its size being as large as...
If even a single feature of Mount Sumeru, with its five peaks, is thus, how much more so are its eighty-four thousand perfect features?
What then can be said of the majesty of his body?
According to the records, the body of Śākyamuni as he appeared in the world was sixteen feet tall; between his eyebrows was a white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*), eight-edged and hollow within.
White as white jade or snow, one zhang five chi in length and five cun in circumference, it curls to the right like a tube of lapis lazuli.
From this, light is emitted, illuminating everywhere without limit. Even the most profound darkness within the Iron Ring Mountains is entirely dispelled wherever this light reaches.
One may thus realize the Dharma through this mark of the hair-tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*) from which the light of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is emitted.

The nature of the dhātus is the domain of a single wisdom. Knowing that the *ūrṇā-kośa* (tuft of hair) between Śākyamuni’s eyebrows is so preeminent, one then knows that the white *ūrṇā* of Amitābha is likewise the most excellent among the eighty-four thousand marks. Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"One who contemplates the Buddha of Immeasurable Life enters through a single mark and excellence; simply contemplate the white *ūrṇā* between his brows until it is perfectly clear and distinct. Thus one sees it.
Regarding the mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows: among the eighty-four thousand marks and signs of excellence, these will naturally manifest.
However, for those at the initial stage of practice, one should first visualize the size of Śākyamuni’s tuft as a standard; by observing it in this sequence, success will be easily achieved.
According to the *Ratnarāja-śāstra*, the single mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows manifested by Śākyamuni’s reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) curls upward to the right;
it is three million six hundred thousand *li* in circumference and diameter. This is barely comparable to a single Mount Sumeru, being only slightly larger than that.
If the white tuft of Amitābha is as large as that, then the white tuft of Śākyamuni is as small as this.
Why does Śākyamuni yield to that Amitābha in this way? Alas, the Buddhas are identical; it is not that they yield to one another.
It is simply that Śākyamuni resides in Saṃbhava, which is a land of defilement. Because the land is defiled, the pure light of the Buddha is easily obscured.
Therefore, when the physical dimensions of the body manifest, they cannot be large; Amitābha resides in Sukhāvatī, which is a pure land.
Because the land is pure, the Buddha’s pure light is easily manifested, and thus the manifestation of his physical dimensions does not result in them being small.
Now, by observing the *ūrṇā-kośa* (hair-treasure) of these two Buddhas, the superiority and inferiority of their respective lands can be clearly understood.
"His dark-blue eyes clarify the four great oceans.
"Dark-blue" (*kan*) is the name for a deep azure color; "oceans" refers to those on the four sides of Mount Sumeru.
His two eyes are long and wide, like two portions of the four great oceans. Thus, both his *ūrṇā* hair-tuft and his eyes are without equal.
Regarding the [two] marks of the white tuft and the eyes: both are set forth in the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra*.
According to this, the pupils of the eyes are deep blue (*kan-sè*) and yet transparently clear; the beauty of these physical characteristics goes without saying.
However, the Buddha’s pure jewel-eyes are eyes retributive of wondrous, luminous wisdom; they see through the ten directions without further obstruction.
As for "obstruction": although it exists within the mental conceptions of sentient beings, the Buddha’s eye perceives it all. Thus, what need is there to discuss the beauty of its physical form?
Even speaking merely from the perspective of its physical appearance, it is a point of universal benefit for those of various capacities.

When Bodhisattvas perceive this physical form, they immediately attain the perfection of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and swiftly accomplish the reward body (*vipākakāya*) of merit. As for sentient beings, some may see it...

Whether one sees [the Buddha] at sixteen feet, or eight chi with the thirty-two marks, one likewise attains sharp and keen faculties, matures as a vessel for the Dharma, and swiftly realizes the bodhicitta of non-retrogression.
One should know that seeing these physical forms is itself seeing the Buddha-mind.
The "innumerable billions of transformation Buddhas within the light" refers to the response-bodies (nirmāṇakāya) of the Buddhas who manifest throughout the worlds.

These are all contained within the eighty-four thousand rays of light that flow forth to fill the realms, each appearing as a transformation Buddha; hence the phrase "within the light. Furthermore, there are two meanings to the term "transformation" (nirmāṇa).
First, the transformation body manifested for oneself is called a *nirmāṇa-buddha*. Second, the transformation [body] that brings others to buddhahood is also called a *nirmāṇa-buddha*.

When Amitābha was on the path of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), he already transformed thirty-six trillion, one hundred and eleven thousand, nine thousand five hundred people so that they reached the stage of attainment together;
how much more so now that he has long since attained buddhahood—he must have divided himself into countless billions.

The response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and transformation Buddhas extensively transform the world; their transformations are even more vast. As for their transforming others, how could they ever be measured by hundreds of millions?

According to this, the two instances of the character "transformation" (*huà*) in the following line correspond to and connect with the three characters "delivering sentient beings. Furthermore, with... [text continues]
In the final phrase, the two characters "xián líng" (all cause) run directly through [the sentence]. It is appropriate to emphasize the aspect of transforming others.

The character "yì" (also) in "transforming the assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise boundless" follows from the light mentioned above. Each transformation-body of a Buddha is uniformly possessed of a corresponding transformation-bodhisattva.
Because he serves as an attendant, he is called an "emanated bodhisattva.

While it should be understood that this bodhisattva is indeed an emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) manifested by Avalokiteśvara, Śrīkūṭa, and others, one must also know that the emanation bodies of these three sages are of one and the same essence. Why is this?
Because within the single Dharmakāya of all Buddhas, there is originally no characteristic of differentiation; yet, it is only when these three aspects are complete that [the manifestation occurs].

The essence of the Dharma is thus complete. Why is this? It is because it corresponds to the principle of the three bodies of a single Buddha. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "transformation" (nirmāṇa), as explained above.
[This is] the fulfillment of the forty-eight vows to deliver sentient beings.
When Amitābha was in the stage of a bodhisattva, he was known as the Bhikṣu Dharmākara. He made forty-eight vows;
I have carefully extracted the text of these vows and set them forth below. I pray that all my fellow practitioners will pay close attention and study them minutely.
"Sentient beings" refers to those born from the conjunction of manifold conditions. Indeed, when sentient beings are born, they originally possess no inherent nature (*svabhāva*);
the nature of that which is produced arises entirely through the meeting of conditions. These meeting conditions are all summoned by karma.
In humans, there are three types of karma: bodily karma, verbal karma, and mental karma. The Buddha established forty-eight vows to gather in and sustain sentient beings.
This causes one to form pure conditions. By teaching the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and the vision of the Buddha, one repents of those defiled karmas.

Once such a superior condition is encountered, one proceeds directly without obstruction, being born straightway in the Pure Land and entering directly into the womb of a lotus. Thus we know that this single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is no small matter;
it is the great causal condition through which Amitābha’s compassion opens the way for salvation.
All nine grades are enabled to reach the other shore.
First, the nine grades are divided into three categories: superior, middling, and inferior. Within each of these three categories, there are again three subdivisions;
this is what is called the nine grades of the lotus. When sentient beings are born in that land, they take rebirth within the interior of a lotus flower. This is said...
This lotus-womb is not the same as being cast into a mother’s womb in this world. For while the latter arises from defiled attachment, the former is born through the transformation of the Dharma.
An ancient sage once made this vow: "May I be born within the Pure Land of the West;
may the nine grades of lotus flowers be my parents. When the flower opens, may I see the Buddha and awaken to non-arising, becoming a Bodhisattva of non-retrogression."
As companions. The first two lines of the prayer signify the intent of taking birth within a lotus. However, the meaning of the word "unborn" (*amṛta*) in the third line is profoundly profound.
According to my analysis, it refers to the Bodhisattva’s thorough penetration of the Dharma-gate of non-self (*anātman*).
For the birth of sentient beings is fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); since there is no birth by way of intrinsic nature, there is likewise no [birth].

The nature of existence is death; birth and entry into death both arise from the aggregation and dispersal of various conditions. If one is separated from these conditions, there is ultimately no birth.
Thus, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* says: "To know that which is illusory is itself to be free from it; no further expedient means need be employed. To be free from illusion is itself awakening."
Nor is it gradual; herein there must be a single great moment of awakening.

If one has not awakened while practicing and realizing in this land, there is no one who will not awaken upon reaching and seeing the Buddha. However, as for the lotuses blooming in that land, they may be slow or fast;
thus, the time of seeing the Buddha is not without its earlier or later. Generally speaking, the lotuses of the highest grade bloom most rapidly, followed by those of the middle grade.
The latter is inferior, for it is slow. Why is this? It is because the sentient beings of this land differ in the sharpness or dullness of their faculties;
they vary in the depth or shallowness of their spiritual power;

and there are those who, having never practiced mindfulness of the Buddha throughout their lives, only begin to recollect him when pressed by the sufferings of the end of life, having been pointed toward it by a virtuous friend.
The valiant and the swift may also attain birth within the lotus; thus, while the birth within the lotus is the same for all, the manner in which the lotus opens differs.
Regarding the stage of rebirth, it is not without basis that one is born [within the lotus];
at the moment of death, auspicious signs will surely manifest before them—whether seeing golden lotuses supporting their feet, or seeing Amitābha coming to welcome them, or...
The brilliance fills the eyes, shining everywhere throughout the infinite expanse; the sacred realms of the Pure Land appear all at once.
One may hear celestial music or perceive wondrous fragrances; at such a time, one knows with certainty that rebirth in the Pure Land is assured.

Furthermore, there are those who committed sins during their lifetime, yet when the moment of death arrives, the horrific visions of hell manifest before them, and fierce flames blaze forth. Riding upon...
As they are about to be overtaken by the void, suddenly a breeze of pure coolness arises to escort them back to the Pure Land.

This occurs because their remorse for their transgressions is so intense and their single-minded resolve so swift that it can counteract the karmic forces accumulated over a hundred years of indolence.

Those who attain rebirth in the lower grades according to the *Contemplation Sūtra* are of this kind; at such a moment, one must rely solely on the recitation of the Buddha’s name and must certainly stand firm.
With a vow as firm and immovable as a mountain, I resolutely resolve to seek rebirth, so that the Buddha’s light may surely shine upon me and the precious lotuses may surely rise up from me.

Thus, when the path of response and invocation meet, one will naturally catch a glimpse of the Original Nature Amitābha, coming from the Pure Land and returning to the Pure Land. At that time, I shall follow behind the Buddha.
Riding upon a precious lotus flower, one is born directly into that land; this is the beginning of the nine grades of rebirth by entrusting oneself to the womb of a lotus.
However, at this time, one beholds the Buddha; one must know that he is none other than the Amitābha of one's own original nature.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings each and every one possess such self-nature merit. Although it is not yet fully realized as an existing reality, it is nevertheless...
It is not produced through artificial conditions or conjunction; rather, it would not manifest were it not for the responsive resonance of that Buddha.
One should know that the merits of the self-nature are nowhere uncreated and nowhere incomplete. To mindfully recollect the Buddha is precisely to create this nature of merit.
To see the Buddha is precisely to possess this nature of merit and virtue. Furthermore, seeing that Buddha’s true body necessarily requires the blossoming of the lotus flower before it can be seen;
once seen, there is no one who does not attain awakening. This is simply a matter of the mutual resonance between the response and the stimulus, whereby the Buddha of nature becomes manifest.
It is like the footprint of a wild goose in the mud: the goose has vanished, yet the impression remains in the mud. If one knows that one's own nature is thus...
When manifested through the seal, the Buddha appears before one all at once; this is not merely a matter of provisional conditions.
Therefore, we know that it is the Buddha of self-nature welcoming the sentient beings of self-nature.

The two characters "xián" (all) and "lìng" (cause to) are extremely direct and decisive. By the power of the ocean of merit of the *tathatā* (suchness) nature, the Buddha has brought forth these nine grades of lotus flowers precisely for the sake of all sentient beings, so that they may all be born therein.

It is simply that if sentient beings believe in the existence of the Pure Land, establish the vow to seek rebirth there, and further apply the power of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*), his faith will be assisted.

This is the power of the vow. Regardless of whether one’s faculties are sharp or dull, and regardless of whether one has committed the ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, or any other extremely grave karmic offenses, all shall attain rebirth while still carrying their karma. Why is this? Because upon reaching the presence of the Buddha, there is none who does not attain awakening;
how much more so for those who can direct their whole heart toward the Buddha, for this constitutes a fierce and intense mind of repentance. Thus it is said:

This is because it cannot harm their faith and vow for rebirth there. One must understand that those nine grades of lotus seats encompass, from above, those of sharp faculties and superior capacity, including all bodhisattvas;
while, from the side, they encompass all sentient beings of middling and inferior faculties.
This is truly the place where all capacities are universally benefited. The "nine grades of lotus flowers" appear in the *Sutra on the Sixteen Contemplations*.
"The other shore" refers to the Pure Land, also named Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). There are nine grades of lotuses, which encompass the ground upon which those who recite the Buddha's name ascend.
In contrast to this, "the shore" is spoken of in relation to the "sea. This land, Sahā, is a realm of regression. [End of excerpt]
Born into death, the cycle of saṃsāra never ceases; all things are suffering. Therefore, it is also specifically called the "Sea of Suffering. Sentient beings sink into its depths;
the river of craving is vast and boundless, and the waves of desire roll on and on. At that time, there shall again come a period of liberation from the kalpa.
That land is Utmost Bliss; it is the stage of non-retrogression, where there is no birth and death, no saṃsāra, and no men.
The women’s passions and desires are purified; all sentient beings are born solely by transformation. Their food, clothing, and requisites are all provided through the Dharma-transformation.
The jeweled towers, pavilions, gardens, groves, and ponds are all the meritorious adornments of the *dharmatā*.

Because of this *dharmatā*, they propagate the joy of the Dharma, such that in every thought-moment they are fully endowed with the bliss of Dharma-joy and the delight of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prīti*).
It increases the path and diminishes birth, bringing joy; thus it continues until the joy of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
It is not like the various joys of humans and devas received in this land; Sukhāvatī is like that, while Saṃbhava (Saha) is like this.

It is precisely the shore upon which sentient beings drowning in this sea of suffering may ascend. Why, then, do sentient beings not seek rebirth there? Moreover, once one has been born in that land, although...

They return once more to the realm of birth and death, entering and exiting the miserable destinies of saṃsāra to deliver all sentient beings and their kinsmen within this Sahā world, never regressing.
This is what is called the skillful means of the vehicle of the non-regressive Bodhisattva for the purpose of transformation and edification.
At such a time, they may depart from the Sahā world or return to the Pure Land, according to their wishes.
How joyful this is! Alas, the appearance of Amitābha in the world truly concerns the inexhaustible, boundless, and inconceivable measure of merit for all sentient beings.

If sentient beings do not believe in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and do not believe in Amitābha, then why would they not believe in the measure of merit within their own inherent nature? Zhongfeng’s “Verses on Cherishing the Pure Land” says: Six...
The Buddha now extends his broad and long tongue, praising together all those in the Sahā world who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

One must believe that within the lotus worlds of the nine grades, there is never a time when the kalpa-vase of spring does not bloom. It is further said: "Kalpa after kalpa, as numerous as motes of dust—though these kalpas be counted to their end, they do not cease.
This is because one’s thoughts are still caught by worldly passions; thus, one remains bound within boundless birth and death."
It is further said: "In the practice of nianfo, one must expect to reach the ultimate point; when that point is reached, both the mind and the recitation are withdrawn together.

Then the winds and waves of the bitter sea of Saṃsāra are stilled, and one sails steadily upon the Prajñā-boat to the Land of Lotus. I pray that all my fellow practitioners will exert yourselves, truly, truly.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha, the Greatly Compassionate and Benevolent Teacher who guides and leads from the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
*Namo* may be translated as *namo*, *nama*, "taking refuge," or "surrendering one's life.
Its explanation has three meanings: first, seeking deliverance for oneself; second, seeking deliverance for others; and third, universally seeking deliverance for all sentient beings.

One seeks perfect fulfillment. To give rise to this mind of perfect fulfillment is itself the bodhicitta. Relying upon the bodhicitta, one recites "Namo Buddha. This is the present method of the Dharma.

It is the meaning of what is called in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "At the very moment of the first thought of generating the mind, one attains perfect enlightenment. This refers precisely to this principle.
Regarding the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), its meaning has already been briefly set forth in the *Pārāyaṇa*. Furthermore, the *Amitābha Sūtra* states:

"From here, passing through a hundred thousand *koṭis* of Buddha-lands to the west, there is a world; that land is named Ultimate Bliss. Thus, Ultimate Bliss is separated from here by a hundred thousand *koṭis*, and the distance is exceedingly vast.
Yet the *Contemplation Sūtra* says that one arrives there in the time it takes to snap one's fingers. It further says, as if [it were] one...

In the space of a single thought-moment, one is immediately born in that land. This is because the mind has no boundaries; it is free from the characteristics of distance and proximity, and free from the characteristics of going and coming.
To be born in a single thought-moment is precisely to be born in the land inherent within one’s own mind.

Thus, having relied upon those superior conditions, one receives the response of the Buddha's grace. What could there be that cannot be reached? [Omitted]. According to this Saha world, it is fully endowed with...
There are four lands: first, the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages; second, the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder;
third, the Land of True Reward Adorned and Unobstructed; and fourth, the Land of Constant Quiescence and Radiance.

Furthermore, the six destinies of hell-dwellers, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas are considered "ordinary beings," while the four destinies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas are considered "sages. Ordinary beings...
The turbid and the holy are pure; one is hidden and the other is manifest. Receiving a segmented body (paricchinna-śarīra), they dwell together with the sages;
hence it is called "the realm where ordinary beings and sages cohabit. This land is precisely the realm of sentient beings of the six destinies.

Having realized the path of skillful means (upāya-mārga) and severed the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa), they receive the dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya), yet one remaining hindrance—ignorance (avidyā)—has not yet been destroyed; hence it is called "skillful means with remainder" (upāya-śeṣa).
This land is the dwelling place of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and other arhats. They receive the reward body (vipākakāya) whose nature is adorned with merit;
therein, matter and mind interpenetrate, the sense faculties and their objects mutually merge, and body and land are non-dual, free from all further obstructions.
This is precisely what is called the Indra’s Net world in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. This land is the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas at the stage of perfection;
therefore, it is called the Land of Real Reward Adorned with Non-obstruction. There is no land apart from the body, and no body apart from the land.
The body and the land are of one suchness; they are profound, eternally quiescent. This is called the Pure Land of the Constantly Quiescent Light. This land is inhabited solely by the Buddha.

Generally speaking, when things are analyzed and divided, they are turbid; when they are perfectly interfused, they are pure. When Bodhisattvas resolve their minds on Bodhi and impartially deliver beings, they have already entered the stage of perfection (*yuanwei*).
The Buddha, however, is the ultimate perfection of this stage. These four lands mentioned above apply equally to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Generally, the lands where ordinary beings and sages dwell together are not exclusively pure; only the Land of Ultimate Bliss is uniquely pure.

The reason it is pure is that while other Buddha-lands are fully possessed of the six realms of existence, in that Land of Ultimate Bliss, ordinary beings and sages dwell together within a single realm, consisting only of the two realms of devas and humans.
The four realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras are entirely absent. Furthermore, it is sustained by the transformative guidance of a single Buddha. Moreover—
There are no malevolent demons or heterodox paths to corrupt and disrupt the Buddha-dharma. Consequently, both the realms of devas and humans alike give rise to the bodhicitta;
they are all born through transformation from lotus flowers, and every interaction among them consists solely of pure and noble companions of the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, as the two realms of devas and humans communicate and travel between one another, the two paths of the ordinary and the sage intersect; the sages manifest in accordance with the times to provide guidance.
In this Sahā world, a Buddha appears but once throughout vast eons; thus, there is a profound disparity between it and those other lands.
Moreover, the sentient beings in those lands possess the two adornments of merit and wisdom equal to those of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is what is meant by "purity within the same land. By this, the nature of the aforementioned three lands can be further understood.
"Guide" (shili) means to lead sentient beings into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, the Buddha is called the Guide.
Because the Buddha dwells in the Pure Land of the Western Quarter and receives and leads sentient beings from this turbid land, he is further called the "Guide Who Leads and Receives."
To bestow all happiness is called the mind of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī-citta*). To extract all suffering is called the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*).

When loving-kindness and compassion universally encompass [all beings] such that bestowing and extracting occur simultaneously, it is called the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion. As the Sūtra says:

"The light of Amitābha Buddha’s loving-kindness and compassion shines universally throughout the Dharma-realm, providing universal protection so that no one shall fall. The power of his compassionate vows pervades..."

It pervades the Dharma-realm, universally encompassing and sustaining all without allowing anything to be lost. The aggregates, sense bases, elements, and the body are everywhere identical to the Dharma-realm;

it causes all to universally awaken to this realization, never permitting regression. For those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they give rise to the mind of perfect liberation and contemplate the Buddha of the Land of Bliss;
thus their merit becomes sublime and their adornments can pervade the entire Dharma-realm. How could there be a Saha world?
The realms are not immediately opened to reveal the Pure Land; how could there be a vow to be born in the Pure Land without immediately going to behold Amitābha?
Alas! Cause and effect are consistently and suddenly perfected, never departing from the present moment.
It simply lies in generating this great mind during the causal stage to truly expand the measure of one's own merit, and in realizing this great mind upon reaching the stage of fruition.
This alone is the means to universally benefit all sentient beings; you must keep this single point in mind and guard against a single misstep—be on your guard!

Once you have ascended to the Land of Ultimate Bliss and entered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), you will attain the stage where the fruits of a sentient being are perfected. May all such people turn their heads and awaken with sudden, vigorous resolve.
